opening.headline: Determine when and how customers should be notified that they are talking to AI in terms of policy needs and trust.
body: If a person's name and photo appears in the customer center chat window, but AI is actually answering the question, is this an efficient service or is it a service that misleads customers? Whether or not to publicize the use of AI is not a matter of technology, but a matter of policy and trust.

In this class, we compare how Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google prohibit deceiving users, and distinguish when notification is necessary and appropriate notification methods. Next, we will explain with examples why chatbots should not pretend to be human, and summarize what notification policies the operating entity should put on top of the provider rules.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the standards and methods for notifying AI use
You can distinguish between cases where notification is necessary and cases where it is not.

screens.title: Do customers know they are talking to AI?
screens.lead: Read a scene from our customer service chat window. It is a good idea to read this while thinking about how this scene will look from the customer's and operator's perspectives.

visual.alt: A scene where an AI icon is hidden behind a chat bubble with a person's photo and name.
labels: How do I get a refund?

paragraphs: The name “Consultant Kim” and a photo of a person appear in the customer center chat window of a shopping mall. Customers think they are talking to a human and send detailed personal information, such as the reason for the refund and their address. But it is AI that actually answers.

The operator may be thinking, “The quality of the answer is good, so why should I report it?” However, customers decide how much to trust, what to say, and what decisions to make differently depending on whether the other person is a human or AI. If you make a conversation while hiding the basis for that judgment, the customer's choice will be distorted.

So the question changes to this: It's not a question of whether this service is efficient, but whether it's misleading customers. This class identifies those boundaries in terms of policy documents and trust.

screens.outro: First, let's think about how we do it in our service.

screens.title: How are you communicating the use of AI in your services?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit an answer, so think of our service first and then click on it.

items.prompt: How are our services informing our use of AI?
items.answer: There are many ways to communicate, such as conversation starters, on-screen badges, and product notations. Whichever method you use, it's important that customers see it before or at the beginning of the conversation. If it is written deep in the terms and conditions, it is similar to not informing the customer.

items.prompt: Where does the notice appear and in what size?
items.answer: Customers will have a hard time noticing if your text is in small font, in the corner of the screen, or disappears after looking at it once. Notice is more important to stand out than to exist. On the conversation screen, check whether it is placed where the customer's eyes are drawn.

items.prompt: If there are cases where you are not notified, what is the reason?
items.answer: Common reasons include concerns about increased bounce or lack of screen space. These costs are real. However, misleading people into thinking you are a person may be misleading, which is prohibited by the provider's policy, so it is not an option that can be omitted just because there is a cost.

screens.outro: Now that we've outlined each person's current approach, let's compare what the provider's policies say about this issue.

screens.title: Notice-related provisions of the provider's policy
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare how the policies of the three providers regulate defrauding users. It is good to note that although the expressions are different, they point in the same direction.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body: Anthropic Usage Policy prohibits impersonating a real person or entity, creating fake personas and accounts to disguise your origin, or misleading you into believing you are interacting with a human being. In the section on disinformation and misleading, examples include running fake entities, such as bots, claiming to be human to deceive users into whether they are interacting with a human. Clearly stated parodies, satire and fiction are not subject to the ban. The policy provides additional use case guidance for consumer-facing chatbots and agents.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: The OpenAI Usage Policy prevents services from being used for manipulation or deception, allowing people to make their own decisions. Unacceptable uses include academic misconduct, fraud and deception such as spam and impersonation. Situations where a non-human entity pretends to be a human being are problematic in this category of impersonation and deception.

tabs.label: Google
tabs.body: Google's Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy prohibits misinformation and misleading practices, including fraud, deceptive impersonation, and misrepresenting the origin of a product. In particular, it specifically describes the act of deceiving the source of a product by claiming that it was created solely by humans. The problem is making service users believe that the content was created by humans.

tabs.label: common ground
tabs.body: All three policies prohibit deceiving users. The specific expressions are different, but the core is the same. This means that you must not make the other person believe that it is a person when it is not, or deceive the person who created it. Therefore, it is safer to design notices in a way that avoids misleading information that is commonly prohibited by the three policies, rather than basing the notice on the wording of one provider.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the direction of the policy, let us specifically distinguish when and how notification is required.

screens.title: When notification is necessary and how to provide notification
screens.lead: When you select an item, an explanation of the circumstances requiring notification and the appropriate method will appear. Substitute the contact points of our service one by one.

items.title: Conversations that may cause customers to misunderstand the other party
items.body: Disclosure is required for interactive services where it is difficult to distinguish whether the customer is human or AI. Representative examples include chat consultation, phone response, and messenger guidance. If the agent's name, a person's photo, or a human-like tone of voice overlap, the likelihood of misidentification increases.

items.title: When a customer directly asks
items.body: When a customer asks “Are you human?”, answering falsely is clearly misleading. Anthropic's Constitution also sets out the principle of not making users believe they are talking to a human and not denying that it is AI to users who seriously ask. Even if the operating entity uses a persona, it must be designed to answer questions truthfully.

items.title: source of product
items.body: Presenting AI-generated articles, images, and reports as if they were created solely by humans is also misleading. Our policies explicitly prohibit this. When publishing content to the outside world, establish a way to indicate that it was created or assisted by AI.

items.title: Method of notification
items.body: The method is clearly determined by the context. There is a conversation starter text, a badge that is always displayed on the conversation screen, and a notation attached to the product. Choose a location and size that the customer won't miss, and allow you to answer truthfully when asked in subsequent conversations.

items.title: Another example of transparency
items.body: Google's Gemini API documentation discloses to users how it detects abuse and that it retains prompts, context, and output for 55 days. Transparency in up front about what a service does is not limited to the fact that you are talking to an AI, but is an effort in the same direction of building trust.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the classification criteria, let's move on to the case and explain why chatbots should not pretend to be human.

screens.title: Commentary: Why chatbots shouldn't pretend to be human
screens.lead: The instructor explains the shopping mall chatbot case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Customer choices are distorted
steps.body: When customers believe that the other person is a human being, they are more likely to hand over their personal information and expect the agent to handle it responsibly. The choice that would have been different if I had known that it was AI was made based on trust. This choice is not made on terms agreed upon by the Customer.

steps.title: This constitutes misleading information prohibited by policy.
steps.body: Anthropic's policy prohibits fake personas that make you believe you are interacting with a human, and OpenAI and Google's policies also prohibit impersonation and misrepresentation of origin. Chatbots that use human names and photos to trick customers into believing they are human are at high risk of falling into this category.

steps.title: When revealed, the problem becomes twofold.
steps.body: If the truth is revealed, the trust customers have placed in the service will be destroyed at once. At the same time, it may be a violation of the provider's policy and may be subject to measures such as access restrictions. Anthropic policy states that if a violation is suspected, it may issue a warning, restrict access or suspend access.

steps.title: Design it like this
steps.body: Do not impersonate your name, photo, or speaking style. Make it clear in the first sentence, “This is an AI counseling assistant,” and add information that you can connect if you need human counseling. The moment when notice is needed is at the very front of the conversation.

steps.title: Answer questions truthfully
steps.body: When a customer asks, “Are you human?” during a conversation, have them answer truthfully. Even if you use a persona, there are no exceptions to this question. If you write these rules down as sentences in your conversation guidelines, they will remain in place even when operators change.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: Notices are not the cost of making your service less attractive, but the cost of gaining customer trust and compliance with your policies. No matter how good the quality of the answer is, it does not justify misleading you. Quality is a separate condition that can be met along with notice.

screens.outro: Now let’s compare the notice policies that the operating entity superimposes on top of the provider rules.

screens.title: Commentary: Provider’s rules and operating entity’s notification policy
screens.lead: Switch between the two views to see the difference between what the provider determines and what the operating entity must decide.

states.label: What the provider decides
states.body: The provider sets the basic principles of its model and service. Anthropic's Constitution places safety and honesty as its core values ​​and embodies the principle of not deceiving people into thinking they are talking to them. OpenAI's Model Specification advocates that people should be able to control how they use AI. This principle determines how the model will behave, and does not determine what text to put on the service screen.

states.label: Determined by the operating entity
states.body: The operating entity superimposes its own notice policy on top of the provider's rules. It is up to the operator to decide what the conversation starter should be, where the badge should be placed, and what notation should be placed on the product. Notices cost money in copy, screen space, and bounceability, but they gain trust and policy compliance. Make the notification policy in writing and set a schedule for inspection with the person in charge. Comparing the two views, the provider's principle is a floor line that the operating entity must adhere to, and the notice policy is a specific promise that the operating entity directly designs on that floor line. Just because a provider requires honesty does not automatically provide a notice on the service screen. Additionally, since the provider's principles cover the behavior of the model, whether a service built on the model attaches a person's name and photo is a design decision for which the operating entity is separately responsible.

screens.outro: I will organize the contents so far from the perspective of trust.

screens.title: Notice is the cost of trust
screens.lead: Let's group the contents of this lesson into one judgment method. Read the paragraph below and move on to the final summary.

paragraphs: Notification of AI use is a promise to customers before it is a legal obligation. Customers need to know who they are talking to so they can decide what to say and how much to believe. Hiding the basis for this decision weakens the foundation of trust, regardless of the quality of the service.

From a policy perspective, the direction is the same. Leaving someone to believe they are a person when they are not is a form of misleading that is prohibited by the policies of all three providers. The principle of high-fat diet is not to have one set format, but to make it stand out according to the context. And when customers ask, we answer truthfully.

There is no denying that notice costs money. However, if you neglect the mistake to save money, you will end up paying a greater cost. It becomes easier to judge if you think of notice as a cost paid in advance to protect trust.

In practice, it is a good idea to bundle the contact list, notice text, display location, question response rules, and inspection cycle into one notice policy. Every time we add a new channel or new creation function, we add a line to this policy, and if we encounter a case of misunderstanding in a customer inquiry, we immediately change the wording and location. A notice is not a phrase that is set once and is done; it is an operational item that is checked again whenever the service changes. Appoint a person in charge, leave a change history, and use customer questions and complaints as the basis for improvement.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Make a list of the touchpoints where it is difficult for customers to recognize that it is AI, and set notification methods and rules for answering questions at each touchpoint.

checks.intro: We compared the wording of the provider's policy. Match each policy with the misleading conduct it prohibits. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Match the provider with the misleading actions that its policy prohibits.
right: Misrepresentation of the source of a product by claiming it was solely created by humans
Making people believe they are talking to a person when they are not
Used to deceive people, such as fraud, impersonation, etc.
checks.correctFeedback: The prohibition language of the three policies was clearly distinguished.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some policies and prohibited activities do not match. Reconsider which of the following terms, including attribution, misidentification, fraud, and impersonation, is closer to that of which provider.
checks.explain: All three providers prohibit deceiving users, and the specific prohibition differs depending on the policy.

checks.intro: Design a paleo diet. You can choose the one that best suits your policy and trust among the customer center chatbot design plans.
checks.q: The customer center chatbot is operated by AI. What is the most appropriate design from a policy and trust perspective?
options: Attach the person's name and photo, but do not reveal them unless the customer asks.
Use a human-like tone of voice and answer that you are a counselor when asked directly.
In the first sentence, it identifies itself as AI and answers truthfully when asked a question.
Notice costs money, so skip it if you think there will be an increase in churn.
checks.correctFeedback: The right design is to reveal it from the beginning and answer questions truthfully.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This design has the potential to cause customers to mistake the other person for a human being.
checks.explain: Making people believe they are human is misleading, which the policy prohibits. You must reveal your name, photo, and tone of voice from the beginning without embellishing it, and answer truthfully when asked.

wrong.0: The name and photo itself create the illusion that the person is a person.
wrong.1: Answering a question falsely is prohibited misleading.
wrong.3: Notice is an option that gains trust and policy compliance, even if it costs money.

glossary.def: Informing service users that AI is involved in their conversation or creation. It allows users to properly judge the opponent and the outcome.
This is a format that announces the use of AI. Conversation starters, permanent on-screen badges, and product notations are present and prominently positioned in context.
The provider's usage policy prohibits deceiving users or pretending to be a person. Operating entities must also design their services within these rules.
This is a state where users can trust the service and leave their judgment to it. Notice is the cost paid in advance to protect this trust.

misconceptions.myth: If the answer quality is good, there is no need to indicate that it is AI.
misconceptions.fact: The problem is not quality, but rather misleading users. No matter how good the quality, making people believe they are human is misleading.

misconceptions.myth: Notification reduces the value of the service.
misconceptions.fact: Notices cost money, such as copy, screen space, and bounceability. However, it is a choice that protects the value of the service because it gains user trust and policy compliance in return.

misconceptions.myth: If you have a persona name, you can pretend to be a person.
misconceptions.fact: There is a difference between writing a persona and pretending to be a person. If a user asks you seriously if you are a human being, you must answer truthfully and not make people believe they are talking to a human being.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Notice is a cost paid in advance to protect trust.
Misleading someone for a person when they are not is misleading, which is prohibited by policy.
High-fat diets are prominently placed in context.
When customers ask questions, answer truthfully.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: At what point in our service is it difficult for users to recognize that it is AI? Just think of one thing: what phrase to place at that point of contact.
